title: Speaking practice: Insulators, Sources and Setting a Mood
description: Eight speaking tasks: present a novel setting, justify an area comparison, argue from temperature data, interpret data about a bridge, narrate a team's solution, persuade classmates, compare two sources and explain mood.

stimuli.title: Present the setting of a novel
paragraphs: Your reading club is discussing a novel called Letters from the Lighthouse. You will present the setting to the club using these notes.
Place: a small, rocky island with a white lighthouse, a post office, and a one-room school.
Time: about 100 years ago.
Weather: fog on most mornings and strong storms in winter.
Daily life: a supply boat arrives only once a week. Families write letters because there are no telephones.

stimuli.title: Which rectangle has the greater area?
paragraphs: Two students each drew a rectangle on grid paper.
Rectangle A: 8 units long and 2.5 units wide.
Rectangle B: 5 units long and 4 units wide.
Kai says: “Rectangle A has the greater area because it is longer.”

stimuli.title: Which material keeps water warmest?
paragraphs: A class tested which material is the best insulator for keeping hot water warm. They filled four identical cups with 200 milliliters of water at 80°C. They wrapped three cups in different materials and left one cup unwrapped. They placed all four cups in the same room and measured the water temperature after 30 minutes.
Wool: 70°C
Paper: 63°C
Aluminum foil: 58°C
No wrapping: 52°C
Teacher's note: A better insulator slows the movement of heat out of the cup.

stimuli.title: How the new bridge changed Marlow
paragraphs: The town of Marlow built a bridge over its river. A visitor to the town museum asks you how life in Marlow changed after the bridge opened. Here is the museum’s list.
Trip across the river: 30 minutes by ferry before the bridge, 5 minutes by car after the bridge.
Families living on the east side of the river: 120 before the bridge, 310 after the bridge.
Shops near the river: 4 before the bridge, 9 after the bridge.
Jobs on the ferry: 15 before the bridge, 0 after the bridge, because the ferry company closed.

stimuli.title: Team Orange saves its poster
paragraphs: You were a member of Team Orange. On the morning of your presentation, the four members carried a poster board to school. Here is what happened.
It started to rain on the way. The poster got wet and the ink on the title ran. There were only twenty minutes before class.

Aisha dried the board with paper towels from the restroom. Marcus asked the office for a marker and rewrote the title. Lin and Tomás found a plastic folder and used it as a cover for the poster. The team arrived at class on time, and the teacher praised their teamwork.

stimuli.title: Pick our class read-aloud
paragraphs: Your class is choosing one book to read together. You read a book called The Goat in the Garden and you think the class should choose it. Here are your notes.
The story is funny: a goat keeps eating the vegetables in a garden.
Each chapter is 6 pages long. There are 15 chapters, so the book has 90 pages.
The main character learns to be patient.

stimuli.title: Which source should we trust?
paragraphs: Your class is studying how historians decide which sources to trust. You are given two sources about the opening of a new market in a town. The question is: How many people came to the opening?
Source A: A statement from the mayor's office, written the next day. It says: “More than 2,000 people came to the opening. It was a great success for our town.”

Source B: A diary entry by a shopkeeper whose store was beside the market entrance. It says: “I counted the people who walked past my door. It rained all afternoon, and I counted only about 300 people.”

stimuli.title: How word choice creates a mood
paragraphs: Your class is learning how authors use word choice to create mood. Read this short excerpt from a story.

The hallway stretched ahead, narrow and gray. Dust hung in the air like smoke. Somewhere behind a closed door, a clock ticked slowly, and each tick seemed louder than the last. Mia's footsteps echoed, and she held her breath.
Your teacher asks you to explain your thinking to the class.

items.stem: Present the setting of the novel to your reading club. Tell where and when the story happens, describe the weather and daily life, and explain how one detail of the setting could cause a problem for the characters.

checklist: I told where and when the story happens.
I described the weather and daily life.
I explained how one setting detail could cause a problem.
I organized my talk in a clear order.
exemplar: Accurately presents place and time from the notes.
Describes weather and daily life with specific details.
Explains a plausible problem tied to a setting detail (a weekly supply boat could mean running out of food; fog could delay the boat).
Organizes the talk with a clear opening, body, and closing.
Uses descriptive noun groups and connectors.

support.clue: After you list the setting details, pick one and ask: what could go wrong because of that?
support.frame: The story takes place on ______, about ______ years ago. The weather is ______. Daily life is ______ because ______. One detail that could cause a problem is ______. This could cause a problem because ______.
support.model: Mentor example (a different setting): “The story takes place in a desert town, about fifty years ago. The weather is hot and dry, with sudden dust storms. Daily life is quiet because most people stay indoors at noon. One detail that could cause a problem is the single well. This could cause a problem because the town would have no water if the well broke.” Now present the setting of Letters from the Lighthouse.

items.stem: Tell Kai whether you agree. Use the area of each rectangle to justify your answer.

checklist: I said whether I agree with Kai.
I found the area of both rectangles.
I used the words area, length, and width.
I explained my conclusion with because.
exemplar: States that Kai is not correct, because the areas are equal.
Shows the area calculations: 8 × 2.5 = 20 and 5 × 4 = 20.
Explains that a longer rectangle can be narrower, so length alone does not decide the area.
Uses area vocabulary accurately.
Speaks directly to Kai with a clear conclusion.

support.clue: Area is length times width. Find the area of A, then the area of B, and compare the two answers. Remember that 2.5 means 2 and a half.
support.frame: I ______ with Kai. The area of Rectangle A is ___ × ___ = ___. The area of Rectangle B is ___ × ___ = ___. The areas are ______, so ______ because ______.
support.model: Mentor example (a different pair of boxes): “Pia says Box B has the greater area. I agree with Pia. The area of Box A is 5 × 2 = 10. The area of Box B is 4 × 3 = 12. Because 12 is greater than 10, Box B has the greater area. I checked both measurements of each box, not only one.” Now answer Kai about Rectangle A and Rectangle B.

facts: Area of a rectangle = length × width.

items.stem: Make a claim about which material is the best insulator. Support it with evidence from the data and reasoning that uses the teacher's note.

checklist: I stated a claim.
I used temperatures from the data as evidence.
I explained my reasoning with the idea of heat moving out of the cup.
I compared my choice to at least one other cup, including the unwrapped cup.
exemplar: States a clear claim (wool was the best insulator).
Cites specific data (70°C for wool compared with 52°C for no wrapping and 58°C for foil).
Links the evidence to the idea that the best insulator let the least heat escape.
Uses the control (unwrapped cup) in the comparison.
Uses scientific vocabulary such as insulator, heat, and temperature, and a claim-evidence-reasoning structure.

support.clue: All the cups started at 80°C. Which cup still has the highest temperature after 30 minutes, and what does that say about heat escaping?
support.frame: My claim is that ______ is the best insulator. The evidence is that the water in the ______ cup was ___°C, while the water in the ______ cup was ___°C. My reasoning is that a better insulator ______, so ______. The unwrapped cup shows ______.
support.model: Mentor example (a different investigation): “My claim is that the thick sock is the best cover for keeping an ice pack cold. The evidence is that the ice pack in the thick sock was 4°C after an hour, while the ice pack in the thin sock was 9°C. My reasoning is that a better insulator slows heat entering the pack, so the pack stays colder. The pack with no cover shows how fast it warms without help.” Now make your claim about the cups of hot water.

facts: After 30 minutes: wool 70°C, paper 63°C, aluminum foil 58°C, no wrapping 52°C.
The wool cup lost 10°C; the unwrapped cup lost 28°C.
A better insulator slows the movement of heat, so the contents stay warmer.

items.stem: Explain to the visitor how life in Marlow changed after the bridge opened. Use at least two numbers from the list, say what each number shows, and tell one thing that was lost.

checklist: I told how the trip across the river changed (30 minutes before, 5 minutes after).
I used at least two numbers from the list and said what each one shows.
I told one thing that was lost or ended.
I used past tense for the changes.
exemplar: Identifies the key change in travel time (30 minutes to 5 minutes).
Compares before and after numbers accurately for at least two lines of the list (for example, 120 to 310 families, 4 to 9 shops).
Says what the numbers show (more people and shops near the bridge) rather than only reading them.
Names one loss (the ferry company closed, so 15 ferry jobs ended).
Uses past tense for what happened and a closing sentence that sums up the change.

support.clue: Pick two lines from the list. For each one, compare the number before and after, and ask what that change shows about life in the town. Then find the line that shows something that ended.
support.frame: Before the bridge, ______. After the bridge, ______. This shows that ______. Another change is ______, from ___ to ___. This shows that ______. However, ______ was lost because ______.
support.model: Mentor example (a different change): “Before the garden club started, the school had 0 vegetable plants. After one season, it had 40 plants. This shows that the club grew a lot. Another change is lunch waste, from 12 bags to 7 bags. This shows that students ate more of the food. However, the soccer team lost its practice field because the garden took the space.” Now explain how life in Marlow changed.

facts: Trip time: 30 minutes by ferry before the bridge, 5 minutes by car after.
Families on the east side: 120 before, 310 after.
Shops near the river: 4 before, 9 after.
Ferry jobs: 15 before, 0 after, because the ferry company closed.

items.stem: Tell the class what happened to Team Orange, as one of the team members. Tell the events in order, say who did what, and explain how the team solved the problem.

checklist: I told the events in order.
I said who did each job.
I explained how the team solved the problem.
I used first-person words such as we and our, and past tense.
exemplar: Narrates the events in order from the rain to the presentation.
Assigns the actions to the correct team members.
Describes the solution and its result (the title was fixed, the poster was protected, the team arrived on time).
Uses first-person plural and past tense with mostly accurate control.
Uses transitions and includes a closing reflection on teamwork.

support.clue: Find the problem first (the rain). Then list what each of the four teammates did, one by one.
support.frame: On the morning of our presentation, we ______ when ______. The problem was that ______. First, ______ did ______. Then, ______ did ______. Finally, ______ and ______ ______. In the end, we ______.
support.model: Mentor example (a different team): “On the morning of our concert, we were getting ready when the power went out. The problem was that our music stands were in a dark room. First, Priya found the flashlights. Then, Ahmed carried the stands outside. Finally, Joy and Ben set up the chairs in the sunny yard. In the end, we played in the sunshine.” Now tell the story of Team Orange.

items.stem: Persuade your classmates to choose The Goat in the Garden. Give at least two reasons from your notes.

checklist: I said which book I want the class to choose.
I gave two reasons.
I used information from my notes.
I finished with a closing sentence.
exemplar: States a clear recommendation for the class.
Gives at least two supported reasons (humor, manageable chapter length, a lesson about patience).
Includes details from the notes (6 pages each, 15 chapters, 90 pages).
Uses persuasive language and connectors.
Concludes with an invitation or summary sentence.

support.clue: Each line in your notes is a possible reason. Choose the two that would matter most to your classmates.
support.frame: I think our class should read ______ because ______. Another reason is that ______. For example, ______. So I hope you will choose it because ______.
support.model: Mentor example (a different book): “I think our class should read The Silver Kite because it is exciting. Another reason is that the story takes place in many countries. For example, the kite flies over mountains, a desert, and a sea. So I hope you will choose it because everyone will learn something new.” Now persuade your classmates about The Goat in the Garden.

items.stem: Decide which source is more trustworthy for answering the question and justify your decision. Compare the two sources and say what other evidence would help.

checklist: I chose a source and explained why.
I compared the author's position and purpose in both sources.
I used details from the sources as evidence.
I explained what other evidence I would want.
exemplar: States a clear conclusion about which source is more trustworthy for this question, with reasoning that is not just opinion.
Compares the sources' authors, purposes, and methods (a mayor's office may want to show success; the shopkeeper describes a count at one door).
Notes limits of each source (the shopkeeper saw only one entrance; the mayor's office has no stated method).
Suggests additional evidence (police counts, ticket sales, photographs, other diaries).
Uses sourcing vocabulary such as purpose, perspective, bias, evidence, reliable.

support.clue: Ask who wrote each source, why they wrote it, and how they counted. Then ask what each author might want the reader to believe.
support.frame: I think Source ___ is more trustworthy for this question because ______. Source A was written by ______, who may want ______. Source B was written by ______, who ______. However, Source ___ has a limit because ______. To be more certain, I would look for ______.
support.model: Mentor example (a different question): “I think the weather report is more trustworthy for deciding about the picnic because it uses measurements. The advertisement for the park was written by the park owner, who may want more visitors. The weather report was written by scientists, who measure wind and rain. However, the report has a limit because forecasts can change. To be more certain, I would check the forecast again the next morning.” Now compare Source A and Source B.

facts: Historians evaluate a source by its author, purpose, perspective, and method.
A source created by an organization that benefits from a particular result may be biased.

items.stem: Explain what mood the author creates in the hallway. Use at least two words or details from the excerpt and explain what feeling each one creates.

checklist: I named the mood.
I used at least two exact words or details from the excerpt.
I explained what feeling each detail creates.
I used a word such as suggests, creates, or shows.
exemplar: Names the mood accurately (tense, uneasy, suspenseful).
Quotes or paraphrases at least two specific details (narrow and gray, the loud clock, echoing footsteps, held her breath).
Explains how each detail contributes to the feeling (narrowness creates a trapped feeling; the louder ticking builds suspense).
Uses literary vocabulary (mood, imagery, suspense) and reasoning words (suggests, creates).
Organizes the explanation with an opening claim and a closing sentence.

support.clue: Pick two words or details that feel unpleasant or quiet. Ask what they make a reader expect might happen.
support.frame: The author creates a ______ mood. One example is the phrase “______,” which suggests ______. Another example is ______, which creates a feeling of ______ because ______. Together, these details make the reader feel ______.
support.model: Mentor example (a different excerpt): “The sun spilled gold across the meadow, and the breeze carried the smell of fresh bread.” “The author creates a peaceful mood. One example is the phrase ‘spilled gold,’ which suggests warm, rich light. Another example is the smell of fresh bread, which creates a feeling of comfort because it reminds readers of home. Together, these details make the reader feel calm.” Now explain the mood in the hallway excerpt.
